Q: Intermittent latency at java.io.RandomAccessFile.open0 while Tomcat classloading? A:

I doubt that is somehow tomcat-related at all. You are correct that `RandomAccessFile.open0` call is not something we would expect to find in threaddumps - this call is relatively cheap, unless it either becomes expensive (AV-software installed) or we perform it too often. I bet you are hitting the second case - according to your threaddump:

at java.lang.ClassLoader.loadClass(java.base@17.0.20/ClassLoader.java:579)
- locked <0x00001000e616ddc8> (a clari5.platform.util.compiler.ClassLoaderImpl)
at clari5.platform.util.compiler.ClassLoaderImpl.loadClass(CharSequenceCompiler.java:584)
- locked <0x00001000e616ddc8> (a clari5.platform.util.compiler.ClassLoaderImpl)
at java.lang.ClassLoader.loadClass(java.base@17.0.20/ClassLoader.java:525)
at com.gen.Foo.someMethod(Foo.java:110)

proprietary clari5.platform.util.compiler.ClassLoaderImpl in the first place delegates loading classes to the parent classloader (parent-first strategy), in general this is OK and the top of threaddump is actually irrelevant, however in case of already running application (warm) that should happen very rarely. The root cause of your issue could be one of the following:

  • you are creating the instance of clari5.platform.util.compiler.ClassLoaderImpl upon every method call/transaction, since you haven't provided the code of com.gen.Foo.someMethod, SO community can't help there

  • implementation of clari5.platform.util.compiler.ClassLoaderImpl is buggy, since it is proprietary, SO community can't help there as well

Q: Why is Collectors.collect not able to infer the types in this stream pipeline? A:

The "obstacle" for the compiler to match the correct types in your example is the lambda. It does not specify its input types and Gatherer is declared with unlimited type parameters, so that doesn't help either.

You have several options to help the compiler with the types:

  1. Specify the type of stream that is gathered in the end:

    String r1 = letters.stream().<String>gather(
    Gatherer.ofSequential(
        (_, t, r) -> r.push(t.toUpperCase())))
    .collect(Collectors.joining());

    In this solution you specify the type parameter for the gather method of the stream - this could be different from the input stream since the method returns a different stream, that could be of another type.

  2. Specify the type parameters for the created Gatherer instance:

    String r2 = letters.stream().gather(
    Gatherer.<String, String>ofSequential(
        (_, t, r) -> r.push(t.toUpperCase())))
    .collect(Collectors.joining());

    In this solution the gather method of the Stream class can find out its result type parameter by the passed implementation of Gatherer - in this case input and output type are String each.

  3. Specify the type parameters of the lambda:

    String r3 = letters.stream().gather(
    Gatherer.ofSequential(
        (Void _, String t, Gatherer.Downstream<? super String> r) -> r.push(t.toUpperCase())))
    .collect(Collectors.joining());

    In this solution the Gatherer can find its type parameters from the passed lambda parameters - the lambda is a Gatherer.Integrator<Void,T,R> instance here. From the type parameters of Gatherer the type parameter of gather() can then be derived.

The shortest version would be solution 1 - but you have to help the compiler at least a bit.

Q: Is there an efficient way to get the first non-zero element in an SIMD register using SIMD intrinsics? A:

  • PCMPEQB/W/D/Q against an all-zero register to get a vector with elements that are all-1 (true) for the zero elements and all-zero (false) for the non-zero elements.

  • PMOVMSKB to turn the vector of all-ones or all-zero into an integer bitmask. (Or movmskps or pd to get 1 bit per dword or qword, instead of per byte, if that makes your bit-scan -> index calculation more efficient, like if you want an element offset instead of a byte offset.)

  • invert that (C ~ operator, asm NOT instruction) to get 1s in the bitmap for elements that were non-zero

  • TZCNT or BSF that integer to find the first (lowest) set bit. Beware of BSF's behaviour if its input is all-zero. But fortunately that's not a problem when the input is an int ~bitmask - the high 16 zero bits become 1s. (An AVX2 version of this with vpmovmskb ymm that filled a whole uint32_t with possibly-1 bits could use ~(uint64_t)bitmask, or just use tzcnt since AVX2 CPUs also have BMI1.)

    In C++20, this is std::countr_one(mask) implemented as std::countr_zero(~mask). std::countr_zero has identical semantics to x86 tzcnt, including for input=0. If you're compiling without BMI1, check the asm to make sure the compiler optimized away any checks for input==0, since uint32_t ~mask is always non-zero for 16-bit vectors.

For example with intrinsics:

int first_nonzero_byte(__m128i v){
    //__m128i v = _mm_loadu_si128((const __m128i*)p);  // for a pointer arg
    __m128i vcmp = _mm_cmpeq_epi8(v, _mm_setzero_si128());
    unsigned bitmask = _mm_movemask_epi8(vcmp);
#ifdef __GNUC__
    return __builtin_ctz(~bitmask);
#else
    return _tzcnt_u32( ~bitmask );
#endif
   // returns 16 if v was all zero so ~bitmask is 0xFFFF0000
}

Compiles on https://godbolt.org/z/Y8vYbsW69 to

# GCC11.2 -O3 -msse4.1
        movdqa  xmm1, xmm0      # missed optimization, should zero XMM1 instead
        pxor    xmm0, xmm0
        pcmpeqb xmm0, xmm1
        pmovmskb        eax, xmm0
        not     eax
        rep bsf eax, eax        # tzcnt on new CPUs, BSF on old
        ret

In GNU C where _tzcnt_u32 won't compile without -march=haswell or something, we use __builtin_ctz. As I said, ~bitmask is guaranteed to be non-zero. tzcnt is encoded as rep bsf; old CPUs will execute it as bsf, producing the same result for non-zero inputs. New CPUs will execute it as tzcnt, which is more efficient on AMD (2 uops instead of 7). Intel executes either as single-uop. GCC uses rep bsf aka tzcnt if you don't tell it a specific CPU to tune for.

For a related function like shown in JATothrim's answer, using only 4 single-uop instructions (actually 2 uops for tzcnt on AMD) instead of 8 instructions including a pblendvb (2 uops on Intel). The shuffle/horizontal-reduction idea in that answer could possibly be useful if you want the element index as a shuffle control vector for vpermilps, but seems sub-optimal vs. this when you actually want a scalar int.

int equal_first_dword_bitscan(__m128i x, __m128i y)
{
    __m128i vcmp = _mm_cmpeq_epi32(x,y);
    unsigned bitmask = _mm_movemask_ps(_mm_castsi128_ps(vcmp));
    bitmask |= 1<<4;    // return 4 if the low 4 bits are all 0
#ifdef __GNUC__
    return __builtin_ctz(bitmask);
#else
    return  _tzcnt_u32( bitmask );  // runs as BSF on old CPUs, don't skip the OR
#endif
}

MSVC doesn't have __builtin_ctz, but will compile _tzcnt_u32 even if you haven't told it the target CPU supports BMI1. If you're definitely only running on CPUs with BMI1, you can leave out the bitmask |= 1<<4; so it will return 32 for not-found.

If you use trailing-zero count in multiple functions, best to wrap that ifdef stuff in a helper function, instead of at each use-case.

If there's only one possible non-zero value (like 1), PCMPEQB against a vector of that so you don't need to invert it later.

If that's the case, consider storing your data in a bitmap in the first place, to decrease your cache footprint by a factor of 8. Then you just TZCNT 64-bit chunks of the array.

Or for a larger array of data, search for the first non-zero vector with SIMD, then TZCNT the first non-zero element of it, if you expect there to be multiple qwords of zeros before the first set bit. Like memcmp does for finding the mismatching byte position.
See Efficiently find least significant set bit in a large array? and How to find the first nonzero in an array efficiently?

BTW, the asm instruction ref manual lists the relevant C intrinsics at the bottom of each entry, and you can search Intel's intrinsics finder by asm mnemonic. (See the x86 tag wiki for links).

Q: Scan directories and delete those that have less than n files A:

This seems to do the job!

Do you see issues with the below?

import os
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

source = Path("./music/")
dest = Path("./musiclight/")
threshold = 7

os.makedirs(dest, exist_ok=True)

for artist in source.iterdir():
    #print(f"je traite : {artist.name}")
    total_files = 0
    if artist.is_dir():
        for album in artist.iterdir():
            if album.is_dir():
                #print(f"je traite : {artist.name} - {album.name}")
                total_files += sum(1 for f in album.rglob('*') if f.is_file())
        if total_files >= threshold:
            print(f"Artist {artist.name} has {total_files} files - ABOVE threshold - To be copied")
            shutil.copytree(artist, dest / artist.name, dirs_exist_ok=True)
        else:
            print(f"Artist {artist.name} has {total_files} files - BELOW threshold - Ignoring")

Q: How to send email with a file attachment using aws ses and java? A:

The solution you posted worked because you added the missing piece of adding the attachment as a separate MIME body part. While that's good, it's still an awful lot of code to achieve something simple.

I want to show you an alternative solution, using the open source Simple Java Mail library (disclaimer: I maintain this library). With it, you can avoid constructing the MimeMessage, MimeMultipart, MimeBodyPart, DataSource, and DataHandler entirely:

List<Recipient> recipients = Arrays.stream(toEmails.split(","))
        .map(String::trim)
        .filter(address -> !address.isEmpty())
        .map(address -> new RecipientBuilder()
                .withAddress(address)
                .withType(Message.RecipientType.TO)
                .build())
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

Email email = EmailBuilder.startingBlank()
        .from(CommonStrings.adminEmailAddress)
        .withRecipients(recipients)
        .withSubject(subject)
        .withHTMLText(textBody.getData())
        .withAttachment(
                inputFileName,
                fileContents.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                "text/csv")
        .buildEmail();

Mailer mailer = MailerBuilder
        .withSMTPServer(
                "email-smtp.<region>.amazonaws.com",
                587,
                System.getenv("SES_SMTP_USERNAME"),
                System.getenv("SES_SMTP_PASSWORD"))
        .withTransportStrategy(TransportStrategy.SMTP_TLS)
        .buildMailer();

mailer.sendMail(email);

The important bit being:

.withAttachment(inputFileName, fileContents.getBytes(UTF_8), "text/csv")

Simple Java Mail builds the correct multipart MIME structure, chooses the encoding, sets the attachment headers, and configures the Jakarta Mail properties for TLS.

Q: Adding a scroll bar for oversized picture to powerpoint A:

This is probably not the answer you are looking for but you can make a faux scrolling bar with shapes and action buttons. The explanation for this is described in the Office page: http://office.microsoft.com/en-us/powerpoint-help/create-a-scrolling-effect-in-powerpoint-2007-HA010245145.aspx

This will allow you to get the feeling of a scrollbar. You can also add separate sections of the picture which becomes visible/invisible when you click the action button instead of showing the next page. You can alter the action by right-clicking the action button and changing the action or you could use a regular button with the shape of an action button with an added hyperlink.

Q: The configuration section cannot contain a CDATA or text element A:

I hads same issue, You should resolve in two simple steps.

1) verify by opening the URL of the Web Service in the Web browser and make sure it is properly responding. (IMPORTANT)

2) If step 1 turned out well, sure there are no typos in the web.config since (happened to me) what can happen is you have been a character "<" or ">" or misspelled most.
